praise.note: The `Pending` absorption story mostly works out: `ok.map(() => pendingErr)` produces `Pending<Settled<number, "inner">, string>` and the type genuinely says the value is a `Settled` — the compiler does not hide the nesting. Calling `.flatten()` on it then recovers the inner `Err` correctly at runtime (`map(->Pending<Err>).flatten() settled ctor => Err`, `isErr => true`), so the escape hatch composes across the async boundary.

The phantom-`E` identity casts in `mapErr`/`orElse`/`flatten` are genuinely sound as re-typings — `Ok` carries no error payload, so there is nothing to leak. The `// SAFETY:` comments explaining each one are the right engineering practice and made auditing them fast.

`Ok`'s short-circuit methods are rigorously lazy: `mapErr`, `orElse` and `unwrapOrElse` never invoke their callbacks on an `Ok` (verified: 0 invocations), so passing an expensive or throwing recovery function costs nothing. That is easy to get wrong and it is right here.

`Ok` is deliberately NOT `PromiseLike`, which means `Promise.resolve(this)` inside `settle()` cannot be absorbed and `await ok` returns the `Ok` itself rather than silently unwrapping. Given how much of the design rests on thenable detection, keeping the settled classes non-thenable is the correct call.

The `NoInfer<U>` on `mapOr`'s `defaultValue` and the `NonThenable<U>` / `SameResolved<A, B>` helpers in types.ts show real care about inference direction — the overload sets steer sync callbacks into sync signatures instead of collapsing everything into `T | Promise<T>`, which is the usual failure mode for libraries of this shape.

`util.inspect`/`console.log` output is clean and unambiguous out of the box (`Ok { value: 42 }`, `Err { error: 42 }`) purely from good class naming and a single public field — debugging sessions read well even without a custom inspector.

The `Err` fast path is allocation-free and provably side-effect-free: `map`, `andThen`, `and` and `flatten` all return `this` (verified `B1`-`B4` all `true`), and the callbacks are never invoked (`B6 map/andThen callbacks invoked count = 0`, and `P8 map fn throw (never called on Err) OK`). Chaining ten combinators onto an error costs zero objects and zero calls — that also gives React-style reference stability for free.

`Err`'s concrete return types are strictly more precise than the abstract base signatures and they are correct: `andThen`/`and` return `Err<InferOk<R>, E>` (correctly dropping `InferErr<R>`, since the callback never runs), `or`/`orElse` return `R` exactly, and `FlattenErr` correctly preserves the outer `E` while flattening the phantom `T` — confirmed by declaration emission: `e.andThen(() => new Ok<boolean, Date>(true))` ⇒ `Err<boolean, string>`, `e.or(new Ok<number, boolean>(1))` ⇒ `Ok<number, boolean>`, `Err<Ok<number,string>, boolean>.flatten()` ⇒ `Err<number, string | boolean>`.

`mapOr` is exactly right on the error path: it returns the default without touching the mapper, verified by the evaluation log `D1 mapOr result = 99 | evaluation log = [ "default-arg-evaluated" ]` — only the (necessarily eager) argument was evaluated, the mapper never ran. `mapOrElse` likewise calls only `defaultFn` (`D2 … order = [ "defaultFn" ]`).

`settle()` is correct and subclass-transparent: it resolves to the very same instance (`H2 settle resolves to same instance: true`) and preserves subclasses (`M3b settle preserves subclass: true`), so `await result.settle()` is a genuine no-op on the settled path.
`isThenable` correctly refuses to assimilate a non-callable `then` — `C11 {then:42} ->  Err` — which rules out the most common accidental false positive (a plain data object with a `then` field).

`orElse` handles the async-recovery case cleanly when given a `Pending`: `new Err("e").orElse(() => Result.try(async () => 0))` returns a well-formed `Pending` that settles to `Ok 0`, with no assimilation weirdness — this is the right primitive, it just needs to be advertised.

The compiler correctly rejects the two most tempting mistakes on this surface: `new Err()` (`TS2554: Expected 1 arguments, but got 0`) and `orElse(async () => new Ok(0))` — both `@ts-expect-error` markers were consumed, so the guardrails genuinely fire rather than merely being intended.

`UnwrapError` keeps a live reference to the originating result (`F4 ue.result is the Err instance: true`) and its stack is rooted exactly at the failing call (`at unwrap (/home/user/antithrow/packages/antithrow/src/err.ts:99:13)` followed immediately by the user frame), so once you know to look at `.result` the debugging experience is genuinely good.

The iterator's cleanup contract is honoured: `return()` after the first yield produces `{ value: undefined, done: true }` and subsequent `next()` calls stay done — which is precisely why `Result.do`'s `iter.return?.()` short-circuit works correctly (`K1 Result.do short circuit: Err bad`).

The SAFETY casts in `Pending.map`/`mapErr` (pending.ts:52,59) are actually accurate, not hand-waves. `Pending<number,string>.map(() => somePending)` is declared `Pending<Settled<string,string>, string>` and at runtime you get exactly an `Ok` wrapping an `Ok` — one level of nesting, precisely as typed. Verified by `tsc --noErrorTruncation ... 08-reveal.ts` printing `Type 'Pending<Settled<string, string>, string>'` and `bun 01-basics.ts` printing `9. Pending.map(fn->Pending) awaited: Ok value: {"value":"deep"} value is Pending? false value is Ok? true`. `map(() => new Ok(...))` gives the same one-level nesting (`Pending<Ok<string,string>, string>`), so the flattening depth is consistent between Result-returning and Pending-returning callbacks.

`flatten()` composes correctly through the async boundary: `Pending<Ok<Pending<Ok(5)>>>.flatten()` awaits to `Ok(5)` (`bun 14-flatten.ts` -> `1. ... -> Ok {"value":5}`), while an unflattened await correctly leaves the inner `Pending` intact (`3. without flatten, inner value stays a Pending: true`). The `map` (nests) vs `andThen` (flattens) distinction also holds exactly on the Pending path (`4. map(->Pending) leaves an Ok<Ok<'x'>>` / `4. andThen(->Pending) fully flattens`).

The inner promise is shared correctly: multiple awaits of one `Pending` return the *identical* `Settled` instance, multiple `.then` calls return distinct promises with equal values, and branching one `Pending` into two independent chains evaluates the source exactly once (`bun 01-basics.ts` -> `3. two awaits give identical Settled instance: true true`; `bun 10-misc.ts` -> `5. source promise evaluated once: 1 branches: 2 11`). `settle()` is a true zero-allocation alias (`settle() === settle() === .promise: true true`).

The constructor is properly type-guarded against a non-Settled payload — `new Pending<number, string>(Promise.resolve(5))` is a compile error (confirmed via a consumed `@ts-expect-error` in 07-typecheck.ts) — and `Pending` composes with the standard promise combinators with exactly right types: `Promise.all([p, p])` is `[Settled<number,string>, Settled<number,string>]`, `Promise.race([p])` is `Settled<number,string>`, `Promise.allSettled([p])` is `[PromiseSettledResult<Settled<number,string>>]`. All asserted with `Equal`/`Expect` and clean at `tsc` exit 0.

The `Result.do` integration is solid on the async path: `yield* pending` works, fail-fast short-circuits on `Err`, and `iter.return()` genuinely runs the generator's `finally` block (`bun 06-asynciter.ts` -> `E. Result.do with yield* Pending: {"value":3}` and `F. fail-fast result: {"error":"bad"} finally ran: true`). The type system also correctly *rejects* the analogous mistake in a synchronous generator — `yield* p` inside `Result.do(function* ...)` is a compile error (consumed `@ts-expect-error` in 13-typecheck2.ts) — catching at build time what would otherwise be `TypeError: yield* new Pending is not a function` at runtime.

`then` is a faithful `PromiseLike` implementation in the details that are easy to get wrong: zero arguments and explicit `null, null` handlers both pass through to the `Settled` value, a throwing `onfulfilled` rejects the derived promise, and `onrejected` receives the raw reason with the union type `PromiseLike<A | B>` inferred correctly (`bun 10-misc.ts` -> `1. p.then() => {"value":1}`, `1. p.then(null, null) => {"value":1}`, `2. then(onfulfilled that throws) rejects: in onfulfilled`).

`unwrap()`/`unwrapErr()` on the wrong branch reject with a real `UnwrapError` carrying the originating result, exactly as the docs promise: `bun 03-poisoned.ts` -> `unwrap() on Pending-of-Err rejects with: UnwrapError true {"error":"failed"}` (`e instanceof UnwrapError` is `true` and `e.result` is the `Err`). The error identity survives the async boundary intact.

`new Pending(anotherPending)` — which the type system permits, since `Pending<T,E>` structurally *is* `PromiseLike<Settled<T,E>>` — behaves sensibly rather than breaking: it awaits to the inner `Settled` and `.map` on it works normally (`bun 01-basics.ts` -> `5b. new Pending(pending) awaits to: Ok {"value":99}` / `5b. .map on double-wrapped works: 100`). A `Pending` stored *inside* an `Ok` is likewise left untouched by `await` (`5. await nested -> ctor: Ok value is Pending: true`).

E defaults to `unknown`, not `any` or `never`, in both factories — the safest possible default. Verified by reveal.ts: `Result.try(() => 42)` is `Settled<number, unknown>` and `Result.fromPromise(Promise.resolve(42))` is `Pending<number, unknown>`. Many Result libraries default to `Error` and lie from the first line.

The three-way overload dispatch is genuinely precise for the common shapes, and the `NonThenable<T>` trick to keep `T | Promise<T>` out of the sync-only signature is clever and works. typecheck.ts asserts and tsc confirms: `() => 42` → `Settled<number, unknown>`, `async () => 42` → `Pending<number, unknown>`, `() => number | Promise<number>` → `Result<number, unknown>`. Getting a sync/async-polymorphic factory to return three different static shapes without any cast at the call site is not easy.

Contextual typing flows the declaring function's return type into E, so `function f(): Result<number, string> { return Result.try(() => 42); }` compiles with no type arguments (typecheck2.ts, tsc exit 0). Ergonomically excellent — the caveat is only that nothing validates it (ok-2).

`fromPromise` attaches its handlers eagerly, so a rejecting promise never produces an unhandled-rejection warning even if the Pending is not awaited for many ticks. runtime2.ts H1 confirms: after a 10ms delay the result still settles cleanly to `Err(Error: x)` with no process-level warning.

`Pending` is re-awaitable and the underlying work runs exactly once: runtime2.ts H2 awaits the same `Result.try(async ...)` three times and reports `fn calls=1`. Wrapping the promise rather than the thunk is the right call here.

Non-Error throws are preserved faithfully rather than being coerced into an `Error`: runtime2.ts E4 shows `throw undefined`, `throw null` and `throw 0` yield `Err(undefined)`, `Err(null)` and `Err(0)` respectively, with the exact value intact. Several competing libraries stringify or wrap these and lose information.

`Result.try` is defensive about its own argument — `Result.try(undefined as any)` returns `Err(TypeError: fn is not a function)` rather than throwing (runtime2.ts G5), and an object with a `then` getter that throws also yields an `Err` (runtime3.ts G6).

The classic generator hazard is handled correctly: `resultDo` captures `next.value` *before* calling `iter.return()`, so a `finally { return somethingElse }` cannot swallow or replace the short-circuit `Err`. Verified — `PRAISE-1: Err("kept")` in 10-findings-repro.ts, where the finally returns 999 and the Err survives intact. Many hand-rolled do-notation implementations get this wrong.

The async path awaits `iter.return()` before resolving, so asynchronous cleanup genuinely completes before the caller observes the result — `PRAISE-2: Err("e") ["async-cleanup-done"]` with a 10 ms `setTimeout` inside the `finally`. The ordering guarantee is stronger than the docs claim.

Only one `iter.next()` call is needed for the entire block, because `Ok`'s iterator yields nothing and `Pending`'s async iterator yields only on failure. That makes the implementation 25 lines and O(1) in driver overhead; measured cost is linear and cheap — 100,000 `yield* new Ok(...)` steps in ~26-31 ms, and short-circuiting out of a 100,000-iteration Err loop in 0.08 ms.

`yield*` composes with user-written helper generators for free: `function* validate(n) { if (n < 0) yield* new Err("negative"); return n * 2 }` can be `yield*`ed from a `do` block and its error type flows into the union automatically (`AF ok -> Ok(8)`, `AF err -> Err("negative")`). This is a genuinely nice emergent property of delegating rather than driving.

Error-union inference is exact, including across heterogeneous Err types and across `Settled`/`Result` unions: a block yielding `Err<never,"a">` and `Err<never,"b">` infers `Settled<number, "a" | "b">`, and `yield*` over a full `Result<number, "r">` union in an async generator infers `Pending<number, "r">` — the async iterator/sync iterator fallback works at both the type and runtime level for all four Ok/Err/Pending-Ok/Pending-Err cases.

The four-overload table in the docs matches the implementation exactly, including the subtle `Generator<never, T, void> -> Ok<T, never>` case that lets a yield-free block keep an uninhabited error channel.

`Ok`, `Err` and `Pending` instances are safely reusable across and within `do` blocks, because `[Symbol.iterator]`/`[Symbol.asyncIterator]` mint a fresh generator per call and `Pending` memoises a single promise — yielding the same `Pending` twice resolves twice from one underlying promise (`AD Ok(18)`).

The sync/async split on the common path is genuinely honest and I could not break it: `ok.map(x => x*2)` is exactly `Ok<number,string>`, `ok.map(async x => x*2)` is exactly `Pending<number,string>`, `err.map(async ...)` correctly stays `Err<number,string>` (it does NOT fabricate a Pending, because the callback never runs), and `res.map(async ...)` is exactly `Err<number,string> | Pending<number,string>`. All four match `instanceof` at runtime (assertions.ts A1-A7 compile clean; `bun runtime1.ts` prints ok=Pending / err=Err / pen=Pending for the async case).

`mapOrElse` with mixed branches is the sharpest piece of typing in the package. `ok.mapOrElse(_e => "sync", async _x => "async")` is typed exactly `PromiseLike<string>` and `err.mapOrElse(...)` on the same call is typed exactly `string` — each class reports which branch IT will actually take, and the runtime agrees (`bun runtime1.ts`: "ok -> runtime: object true" / "err -> runtime: string \"sync\"", and the reverse for async-default/sync-map). The `SameResolved<A,B>` helper is a clean way to express "same after await" and it does reject genuinely mismatched branches on all four receivers.

`Ok.map` with a `string | Promise<string>` callback distributes to exactly `Ok<string,string> | Pending<string,string>` — the union return type is faithfully reflected in the union result type, and the runtime picks the matching arm per call (`bun runtime1.ts`: ok(2).map(un) -> Ok, ok(3).map(un) -> Pending). Very few Result libraries model this at all.

The impossible-side unwraps are typed `never` rather than `T`: `err.unwrap()` is `never` and `ok.unwrapErr()` is `never`, so dead code after them is visible to the checker, and on the union they collapse cleanly to `number | PromiseLike<number>` / `string | PromiseLike<string>`.

`Ok.unwrapOrElse(async () => 0)` is typed `number`, not `PromiseLike<number>` — the library correctly notices that an `Ok` never invokes the fallback and so never becomes async. Runtime confirms (`number 1`). The same care shows in `Err.mapOr(0, async x => x*2)` typing as `number`.

`orElse` narrows the whole union cleanly: `res.orElse(recover)` on `Result<number,string>` with a `(e: string) => Result<number, boolean>` gives exactly `Result<number, boolean>` — a single tidy type, no leftover arms. This is the behaviour `or` should have had.

`settle()` collapses correctly across the union — `PromiseLike<Ok<...>>` on Ok, `PromiseLike<Err<...>>` on Err, and `PromiseLike<Settled<number,string>>` on the union (union reduction works because the classes are declared covariant with `out T, out E`). The explicit variance annotations are a good call and they do real work here.

Heterogeneous chains stay honest end to end: `new Ok<number,string>(2).map(x => x+1).map(async x => x*10).andThen(x => new Ok<string,boolean>(String(x))).mapErr(String)` types as `Ok -> Pending -> Pending -> Pending` and `bun unsound2.ts` prints exactly `Ok Pending Pending Pending`, settling to `Ok {"value":"30"}`. Once a chain goes async it stays async in both the type system and the runtime, with no drift.

`andThen`/`and` get the error algebra right per class: `Ok.andThen` passes `R` through verbatim (dropping its own unreachable `E`), `Err.andThen` keeps `E` and only borrows `InferOk<R>`, and `Pending.andThen` correctly unions to `E | InferErr<R>` because a Pending really can settle either way.

Narrowing through the three guards is complete and correct on the happy path: after `isOk()` false and `isErr()` false the union really does narrow to `Pending<T,E>`, `!r.isPending()` gives exactly `Ok<T,E> | Err<T,E>`, `.error` is correctly rejected on the non-Ok branch, and a fourth `const _: never = r` compiles — full exhaustiveness without a discriminant field (01-narrowing.ts, 10-exhaustive.ts, both tsc exit 0).

Three independent narrowing mechanisms give identical results: the `is*()` methods, `instanceof Ok/Err/Pending`, and `"value" in r` / `"error" in r` / `"then" in r` all narrow to the same types, including in the negative branches and for exhaustiveness. That parity is unusual and means users' instincts all work (01-narrowing.ts, 11-generic-and-in.ts).

The guards are plain methods returning constants rather than `instanceof` checks, so they survive the duplicate-package hazard that breaks `instanceof`. Demonstrated with two live copies of the library: `same class object? false`, `fromDist instanceof OkSrc: false`, but `fromDist.isOk(): true` (16-dual-copy.ts).

The `out T` / `out E` annotations are doing real work in the right direction: they *reject* the bivariance TypeScript would otherwise permit on phantom parameters. `Ok<number,string>` is not assignable to `Ok<number,boolean>`, `Err<never,string>` not to `Err<never,number>`, `Pending<number,string>` not to `Pending<number,boolean>`, and `Ok<Animal,never>` not to `Ok<Dog,never>` — all verified as errors (04-variance.ts).

Covariance makes annotation-free code flow correctly: `b ? new Ok(1) : new Err("e")` infers `Ok<number,never> | Err<never,string>` and assigns cleanly to both `Result<number,string>` and `Settled<number,string>` with no casts and no explicit type arguments (12-inference-flow.ts).

The phantom parameters are not exposed as phantom *data*: a narrowed `Err<number,string>` has no `.value` property and a narrowed `Ok<number,string>` has no `.error` property (both rejected), while `Err#unwrap()` and `Ok#unwrapErr()` are honestly typed `never` (14-phantom.ts).

Inferred type predicates (TS 5.5+) propagate through the guards, so the common cases just work with no hand-written predicate: `results.filter(r => r.isOk())` yields `Ok<number,string>[]`, `.filter(r => r.isErr())` yields `Err[]`, `.filter(r => r.isPending())` yields `Pending[]`, `.find(...)` yields `Ok | undefined`, and `.every(r => r.isOk())` narrows the array itself (03-filter.ts, 12-inference-flow.ts).

`Settled<T,E>` is assignable to `Result<T,E>` and `Result<T,E>` is correctly *not* assignable to `Settled<T,E>`, so the settled/pending distinction is enforced in the direction that matters (04-variance.ts).

FlattenOk preserving the inner *variant class* is strictly more precise than both Rust's `Result::flatten` and this library's own legacy `flatten` (which both return the full `Result<U, E|F>` union). `new Ok(new Ok(42)).flatten()` is `Ok<number, never>` and `Ok<Err<never,string>, E>.flatten()` is `Err<never, string|E>` — no needless re-narrowing at the call site. Verified: reveal2.ts(29,7) 'Ok<number, never>'.

Unioning the two error types as `E | F` is the right TypeScript adaptation of Rust, whose `Result::flatten` requires both error types to be *identical*. The documented headline case is exactly right: `Result<Result<number,string>, boolean>.flatten()` is precisely `Result<number, string | boolean>` (reveal2.ts(24,7): 'Pending<number, string|boolean> | Err<number, string|boolean> | Ok<number, string|boolean>'), matching the JSDoc example at base.ts:176-181.

flatten is idempotent-safe on over-application: triple-flattening a doubly-nested value both typechecks and behaves. `Ok<Ok<Ok<number,never>,never>,never>` flattens to `Ok<Ok<number,never>,never>` then `Ok<number,never>` and a third call is a stable `Ok<number,never>` (reveal4.ts lines 29/30/32), with runtime agreeing (runtime1.ts case 7).

The deferred conditional types stay usable behind generics — `function flattenAll<T, E>(rs: Result<Result<T, E>, E>[]): Result<T, E>[] { return rs.map(r => r.flatten()); }` and `function genericFlatten<T, E>(r: Ok<T, E>): Result<unknown, unknown> { return r.flatten(); }` both compile with no assertions (reveal4.ts, no diagnostics on those lines). Conditional-type-heavy APIs frequently fail this test.

Pending.flatten() handles every settled shape correctly, including the awkward ones: inner Err short-circuits (runtime1.ts 8c/8d), a raw `Promise` payload is correctly NOT mistaken for a Result and survives as a Promise inside the Ok (8f), and nested Pending chains collapse to the exact depth the type predicts (8b, 8e, runtime3.ts case 4/5).

Every `as unknown as` cast in the three flatten implementations carries an explicit `// SAFETY:` comment explaining the invariant (ok.ts:106, err.ts:94, and the assimilation notes at pending.ts:52/59). Two of those invariants turn out to be conditional rather than absolute (findings ok-1/ok-2), but the practice of writing them down is what made the gap findable.

`await` on a `Result` union collapses to exactly `Settled<T, E>` with no helper call — verified `Expect<Equal<Awaited<Result<number,string>>, Settled<number,string>>>` passes (19-praise-and-merge.ts, TSC EXIT=0). This is the payoff of making `Pending` a member of the union rather than a parallel type, and it is genuinely nicer than neverthrow's `ResultAsync`, where you must remember which type you are holding. `Promise.all` over a mixed `Result[]` also happens to work correctly as a settle-all (02-combine.ts), because `Ok`/`Err` are non-thenable and pass through.

`Result.try` preserves synchronicity in the type rather than pessimistically returning the full union: `Result.try(() => 1)` is `Settled<number, unknown>` and `Result.try(async () => 1)` is `Pending<number, unknown>` (19-praise-and-merge.ts). The `NonThenable<T>` overload trick that achieves this is careful work, and it means the three-state model does not tax code that never goes async.

The unannotated default error type is `unknown`, not `any` — `Result.try(() => JSON.parse("{}") as {a:number})` reveals as `Settled<{a:number}, unknown>` (14b.ts). The default is the safe one; the hole in ok-1 only opens when a user explicitly asserts otherwise.

`Result.do` (neverthrow's `safeTry`) is well-typed and precise about reachability: yielding a statically-known `Ok<number, "E1">` contributes nothing to the error channel (because `Ok[Symbol.iterator]` is `Generator<never, T, void>`), while yielding a real `Err` or a `Result` union contributes its error type. `Result.do` over a `Result<number, string>[]` correctly infers `Pending<number[], string>`, and the sync/async generator overloads keep sync flows sync (03-combine-types.ts, 19-praise-and-merge.ts). Getting the `never`-yield encoding right is the hard part of this pattern and it is done correctly.

`UnwrapError` carries the offending result as a typed `Settled<unknown, unknown>` property rather than only a string, so a catcher can re-inspect the failure programmatically (19-praise-and-merge.ts, 12-serialization.ts). Most libraries throw a bare `Error` here.

`Result` is a merged type alias and value under one name, so a single `import { Result }` serves both `Result<T, E>` annotations and `Result.try(...)` calls — no separate namespace import, which is a small thing that shows up on every file in a codebase.

The `SafetyE`/`SameResolved`/`FlattenThenable` type helpers and the `// SAFETY:` comments on every internal cast show real discipline about where the unchecked assertions live. The casts that exist are localized, annotated, and each one is defensible (casting an uninhabited `never` channel).

Every runtime-value comment in base.ts's @example blocks is correct — all 15 checked (`// 10`, `// 0`, `// 5`, `// "failed"`, `Ok(42)`, `Error("failed")`, etc.) matched observed output exactly on the first run (01-base-runtime.ts). The value-level documentation is genuinely trustworthy; only the type-level annotations drift.

The `@throws Errors thrown by \`fn\` are not caught.` claim is accurate for every method that carries it, and holds for the async case too: `Ok.map(async () => { throw ... })` produces a `Pending` whose promise rejects rather than an `Err` (13-throws-and-maporelse.ts). This is the library's most consequential design decision and the docs state it consistently in base.ts, the README warning block, result.ts's Result.do JSDoc, and reference/result.md — four independent places, all agreeing.

errors.ts's UnwrapError example is exactly right, including the type claim `error.result; // Settled<unknown, unknown>` which passes a strict `Equal` assertion (06-other-jsdoc.ts). The message strings quoted in unwrap-error.md L34-35 also match verbatim, and `pending.unwrap()` on an Err branch really does reject with an `UnwrapError` as L36 promises.

The `isPending` example in base.ts compiles exactly as written, including the non-obvious part: `const result: Result<number, string> = Result.try(async () => 42)` type-checks because `E` is inferred contextually from the annotation, and `await result` inside the guard is precisely `Settled<number, string>` as the comment claims. That is a subtle inference path to get right in a doc example.

`mapOrElse`'s contract — "Both functions should return the same resolved type `U` (`U` or `PromiseLike<U>`)" — is not just documented but actually enforced by the `SameResolved<A,B>` helper. A mismatched pair is rejected with a readable three-overload error, and the sync-default/async-fn mix the doc says is allowed correctly yields `PromiseLike<number>` (17-maporelse-contract.ts). Documented invariants backed by the type system are rare.

Concrete-class methods inherit their base.ts JSDoc on hover, so `new Ok(1).map`, `.and`, `.or`, `.settle` all surface the abstract class's documentation despite carrying none of their own (15-hover-coverage.mjs). The single-doc-surface design in base.ts is the right call, and it works.

Every README code fence compiles: the quick-start ConfigError pipeline, the SyntaxError warning block, the async `Result.do` (including the `// Pending<number, never>` claim, which passes a strict `Equal` assertion), all three static-constructor snippets, and the full "Settle at the App Boundary" handler with its five yielded steps. The README-to-runtime claims also check out (`ok(4)`, `ok(5)`, `5`), as does tutorial/02's promised program output.

The docs site is unusually well-structured for a library this size: a genuine Diátaxis split, a per-shape availability matrix in methods.md, and an explicit "## Throws" section on every reference page. The `settled.md`, `pending.md`, `unwrap-error.md`, and `result.md` examples all compile unmodified. The explanation section (three-state-model, eager-vs-lazy, when-not-to-use) is honest about trade-offs and names competitors accurately rather than strawmanning them.

`Result.do` composes flawlessly across package boundaries, in both sync and async form, with exact error unions. `Result.do(function*(){ const raw = yield* safeDecode(...); const obj = yield* SafeJSON.parse<{n:number}>(raw); return obj.n })` typechecks to precisely `Settled<number, URIError | SyntaxError>`, and the async variant mixing `@antithrow/node`'s `Pending` readFile with a std `Settled` typechecks to `Pending<number, NodeJS.ErrnoException | SyntaxError>` — verified tsc EXIT=0 in 14-do-with-siblings.ts, with correct short-circuiting at runtime (14b-do-runtime.ts). Getting a generator-based do-notation to unify a `Pending` and a `Settled` in one `yield*` chain, with no annotation from the caller, is genuinely hard and it works.

The iterator/duck-typing parts of the design are cross-realm safe by construction. In 01-cross-realm.ts, `Result.do` over an `Ok`/`Err` from a *different* copy of the library still yields `Ok 7` / `Err boom`, and `isOk()` still returns true, because those paths use structural `Symbol.iterator`/method dispatch rather than `instanceof`. `flatten` is the sole exception — which is what makes the fix scoped and cheap.

Narrowing through a long cross-package chain is exact and exhaustive. After `parsePort().map().andThen(fetch).andThen(Response.json)` and an `await`, `config.error` narrows to precisely `SyntaxError | TypeError | DOMException | "invalid-port"` — the original string-literal error from four steps upstream survives — and the `else` branch after `isOk()`/`isErr()` is provably `never` (12d-narrow.ts, tsc EXIT=0). Error-union accumulation through mixed sync/async combinators is where most Result libraries leak, and this one does not.

The three lint rules are carefully built where it counts. `no-throwing-call`'s `isImplicitGlobal` correctly refuses to fire on a shadowed `fetch`/`JSON` (so the tutorial's own `import { fetch } from "@antithrow/std"` does not self-report), `no-unused-result` recurses through conditional/logical/sequence/as/non-null/chain expressions rather than only checking the top node, and its `needsParentheses` helper gets the `void (...)` fix right for `as`/ternary operands. The `getResultVariant` MIXED-on-Pending guard also correctly refuses to autofix `unwrap()` on a possibly-async result.

`@antithrow/std`'s `structuredClone` hand-rolls try/catch rather than fighting the type system with a cast — which turned out to be the correct call, since `Result.try` genuinely cannot express it (rc-5). Preferring honest, boring code over an `as unknown as` is the right instinct, and it left a clean signal about a real core limitation.

The consumer packages are almost cast-free. Across ~1,000 lines of production source in four packages, there is exactly one Result-related cast (`error as DOMException` in structured-clone.ts:32) and zero `@ts-expect-error`/`@ts-ignore`/`as any`. For a library whose whole job is type gymnastics, that is a strong signal the everyday surface is genuinely usable.

Peer-dependency hygiene on std/node/standard-schema is right: `antithrow` is a `peerDependency` (not a bundled `dependency`), which is the correct choice for a type-identity-carrying core and avoids forcing duplicate copies in the common case.

The Settled wrapper is deliberately NOT thenable (only Pending implements `then`), which is the single most important design decision in the async model: it means `this.promise.then(settled => ...)` inside Pending never accidentally assimilates a Result. Verified in 04-thenable-payloads.ts section U — awaiting a `Pending<number, Promise<string>>` yields an `Err` whose `.error instanceof Promise` is still `true`, i.e. a promise-typed payload survives a full await round-trip unmangled. Many Result-for-JS libraries get this wrong.

The type-level model of thenable payloads is genuinely precise, not merely permissive. tsc EXIT=0 on 06-typecheck.ts confirms that `Ok<Pending<number,string>, string>.map(v => v)` is typed exactly `Pending<Settled<number,string>, string>` — and 04-thenable-payloads.ts section T confirms the runtime produces exactly that (an Ok wrapping a Settled). The `FlattenThenable`/`NonThenable`/`SameResolved` overload machinery in types.ts is doing real work to keep the declared type honest through promise assimilation.

`Result.fromPromise` and `Result.try` correctly and unconditionally capture rejections and synchronous throws into `Err` — the primary entry points into the library are sound, and the whole poisoned-Pending problem is confined to post-construction chaining.

`Result.do` explicitly calls `iter.return?.()` on the fail-fast path (result.ts:96 and result.ts:108) so user `finally` blocks run on early exit. That is a subtle correctness detail most generator-based do-notation implementations skip.

`UnwrapError` carries the entire settled `Result` on `.result`, not just the raw payload. Even with the `unknown` typing critiqued in ep-8, this is strictly more recoverable than what most comparable libraries expose, and it makes `error.result.isErr()` narrowing work in a catch block.

The `@throws Errors thrown by `fn` are not caught.` tag is present on every single affected method in base.ts (map, mapErr, mapOr, mapOrElse, andThen, orElse, unwrapOrElse). The stance is stated up front on each method rather than buried in prose — the problem found in this audit is that the stance means two different things on two paths, not that it was left undocumented.

`sideEffects: false` is genuinely correct and empirically effective. There are no top-level side effects anywhere in dist (base.js is a bare class, errors.js a class extending Error, result.js a plain object literal), and a bundle importing all five public symbols but using none shakes to 20 bytes: `unused: min=20B gz=54B`. Many libraries set this flag aspirationally; here it is earned.

The shipped size is excellent. The complete public API bundles to 3,001 B minified / 873 B gzip (esbuild, esm, minify). For a library offering a full tri-state Result algebra with sync/async unification, sub-1 KB gzip is a strong number.
The `types` condition is correctly placed FIRST in every exports entry — the single most commonly botched detail in exports maps, and it is right here and in all four sibling packages.

No wildcard or deep-path exports: internal modules (utils.js, base.js, types.js) are genuinely unreachable from outside, which is real encapsulation rather than convention. Verified — `import type { FlattenOk } from "antithrow/dist/types.js"` is an error. (The flip side is pkg-3, but the encapsulation instinct itself is right.)

JSDoc placed on the abstract base class propagates correctly to consumers through the emitted declarations, without duplication in each subclass. LanguageService quickinfo on `Ok.map`, `Ok.unwrapOr` and `Ok.flatten` all return full documentation despite ok.d.ts carrying no comments — a nicely economical documentation architecture.

The multi-overload signatures survive declaration emit intact and legibly — e.g. ok.d.ts keeps all three `map` overloads, all three `mapOr`, all three `mapOrElse`, and result.d.ts keeps all four `resultDo` overloads, with the private `declare function` + `export declare const Result: { try: typeof resultTry; ... }` pattern correctly hiding the implementation names behind `export {}`. No `any` leakage anywhere in the shipped declarations.

`files: ["dist"]` is tight and correct: 30 files, zero test files, zero tsconfigs, zero stray source. `publint` runs in the package's own lint script, showing packaging is something the project already thinks about — it just needs attw alongside it.

Packaging is consistent across all five workspace packages (same exports shape, same `files`, same `sideEffects`, `main`/`types` fallbacks present everywhere for node10). Whatever is fixed here can be fixed uniformly, and the sibling packages correctly declare `antithrow` as a peerDependency rather than a dependency — which avoids duplicate-copy class-identity hazards of the kind pkg-5 describes.

The tri-state unification genuinely pays for itself: `await` works uniformly on any `Result<T,E>` and yields a `Settled<T,E>`, so the sync/async fork that forced legacy users into `Result` vs `ResultAsync` (and the `toAsync()` bridge, and the six `*Async` methods 2.0.0 had to delete) simply disappears. Verified in 20-await-unification.ts — `Ok -> await -> Ok 1`, `Err -> await -> Err boom`, `Pending -> await -> Ok 3` through one loop over `Result<number,string>[]` — and at the type level in 20b-await-types.ts (`Equal<typeof await r, Settled<number, string>>`, EXIT=0). Legacy `ok(1)` has no `.then` (`typeof undefined`), so no such shared path existed.

`Result.try` now handles async functions correctly, closing a nasty legacy footgun. `LResult.try(async () => { throw new Error("boom"); })` returns `Ok` wrapping a rejected promise and produces an unhandled rejection; core `Result.try` on the identical callback returns `Pending` that settles to `Err -> boom`. Observed in 14-legacy-try-async.ts, including the `!! UNHANDLED REJECTION: Error: boom` line from the legacy path.

`UnwrapError` is a real improvement over legacy's `new Error(\`Called unwrap on an Err value: ${String(this.error)}\`)`: it has a stable `name`, carries the offending result on `.result`, and — importantly — stops stringifying the error payload into a message (legacy's `String(this.error)` would happily leak a whole error object into a log line). Observed in 02-dropped-runtime.ts: `new unwrap throws: UnwrapError | Called unwrap() on an Err value`.

The two generations are cleanly isolated at the type level, in both directions and across every entry point I could think of — assignment, `andThen`/`and`, `Result.do`, `chain`, and the namespace statics. All twelve `@ts-expect-error` markers in 05-interop-types.ts fired (EXIT=0). Given that both generations export classes literally named `Ok`, `Err`, and `Result`, accidental structural interop would have been very easy to ship and would have been genuinely dangerous; the extra `isPending`/`settle` members close it off by construction.

`Result.do` preserves the subtle bits of `chain` that are easy to lose in a rewrite: `iter.return?.()` is still called on fail-fast so user `finally` blocks run (verified for both sync and async generators in 15-chain-vs-do.ts), thrown exceptions are still deliberately *not* converted to `Err`, and the multi-`Err` union inference from the 2.0.0 `chain` fix carries over intact (`Settled<number, "a" | "b">`).

The deprecation discipline on the legacy subpath is better than most projects manage — 7 of 9 exports produce real editor strikethrough via `@deprecated` (14 suggestion diagnostics across import specifiers and call sites), the subpath is properly gated in `package.json` `exports` (deep imports like `antithrow/dist/legacy/index.js` correctly fail with `ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND`), and the ESLint plugin's path-based exclusion is careful enough to handle nested `node_modules` layouts. The `ok`/`okAsync` gap (lm-3) is an overload-mechanics slip, not a lack of care.
